articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $4.2M tourism contract renewal raises questions about oversight
articles.dek: The Tourist Development Council is set to vote Thursday on extending its marketing agreement with a firm that has never faced a competitive bid process. County commissioners say they weren't consulted.
brief: The Tourist Development Council will vote Thursday on a $4.2 million contract extension with Paradise Coast Marketing, a firm that has held the county's destination marketing contract since 2019 without ever facing competitive bidding.
Three Escambia County commissioners told The Flightline they were not consulted about the renewal and learned of it through the TDC's published agenda.

County procurement policy requires contracts over $50,000 to go through competitive solicitation, but TDC agreements have historically been treated as exempt under a 2017 interpretation that tourism marketing constitutes 'professional services.'
articles.body:
The conference room on the fourth floor of the Escambia County Central Office Complex seats maybe forty people. On Thursday morning, it will hold the nine members of the Tourist Development Council, a handful of staff, and whoever else shows up to watch them vote on spending $4.2 million.

The agenda item runs three pages. It recommends extending the county's destination marketing contract with Paradise Coast Marketing through September 2029. The firm has held this contract since 2019. It has never been put out for bid.

Three Escambia County commissioners told The Flightline this week they did not know the renewal was coming until the TDC agenda posted last Friday.

"I found out the same way you did," said Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach. "By reading the agenda online."

The contract

Paradise Coast Marketing is a Fort Walton Beach firm that handles destination marketing for several Northwest Florida counties. Under its current agreement with Escambia County, the company manages advertising campaigns, social media, travel industry outreach, and the Visit Pensacola brand.

The contract pays Paradise Coast $1.4 million annually, funded entirely through the county's share of the tourist development tax—the so-called "bed tax" collected on short-term rentals and hotel stays. The proposed extension would run three years at the same rate, bringing the total contract value since 2019 to $11.2 million.

TDC Executive Director Dana Reynolds said the renewal reflects satisfaction with Paradise Coast's performance.

"We've seen consistent growth in visitor spending and overnight stays," Reynolds said in a phone interview Tuesday. "The metrics support continuing this relationship."

She said the TDC's legal counsel advised that destination marketing contracts qualify as professional services under Florida Statute 287.055, which exempts certain specialized work from competitive bidding requirements.

The exemption

That interpretation dates to 2017, when the TDC first argued that tourism marketing requires specialized expertise analogous to architecture or engineering—the fields the statute explicitly names.

The county attorney's office signed off on that reading at the time. But the current county attorney, Alison Rogers, said her office has not reviewed the question recently.

"That determination was made before my tenure," Rogers said. "If the board wanted us to revisit it, we would."

Escambia County's procurement code requires competitive solicitation for any contract over $50,000. The code lists several exemptions, including professional services as defined by state law. Whether tourism marketing fits that definition is a matter of interpretation.

At least one Florida court has ruled narrowly on the question. In a 2014 case involving Brevard County, an appeals court found that marketing services did not automatically qualify for the professional services exemption, though the ruling turned on specific contract language rather than establishing a broad precedent.

Reynolds said she was not aware of that case.

The commissioners

County commissioners do not sit on the Tourist Development Council. The TDC operates as an advisory body with its own budget authority over bed tax revenues, which state law restricts to tourism-related purposes.

But commissioners approve the annual tourist development plan and have historically exercised oversight through budget hearings and occasional audits.

Commissioner Bergosh said that oversight has weakened over time.

"There's been a drift toward treating the TDC like it's fully autonomous," he said. "It's not. Those are public dollars."

Commissioner Lumon May, whose District 3 covers much of central Pensacola, said he would have expected consultation on a multimillion-dollar renewal.

"I'm not saying there's anything wrong with the contract," May said. "I'm saying I'd like to have known about it before it hit the agenda."

Commissioner Steven Barry declined to comment on the specific contract but said he supports "regular review of all significant expenditures."

Commission Chair Robert Bender and Commissioner Mike Kohler did not respond to requests for comment.

The questions

The Flightline requested copies of Paradise Coast Marketing's annual performance reports and any internal evaluations conducted by TDC staff. Reynolds said performance data is compiled quarterly and presented to the council but that formal written evaluations do not exist.

"Our assessment is ongoing," she said. "It's not a single document."

Asked whether the TDC had ever considered soliciting competing proposals, Reynolds said the question had come up informally but never reached the agenda.

"You'd have to ask the council members about that," she said.

TDC Chair Marcus Chen, who owns three hotels on Pensacola Beach, did not return calls this week. Vice Chair Linda Patterson, a vacation rental manager, said she supports the renewal but understands why commissioners might have questions.

"Transparency is important," Patterson said. "If they want to come to the meeting and ask questions, they should."

Thursday's vote

The TDC meeting begins at 9 a.m. in Room 410 of the Central Office Complex, 221 Palafox Place. The contract renewal is item 7B on the agenda. Public comment is permitted but limited to three minutes per speaker.

If approved, the contract would take effect October 1 and run through September 30, 2029.

Commissioner Bergosh said he plans to attend.

"I just want to understand the process," he said. "That's not an unreasonable thing to ask."

articles.label: Analysis
articles.headline: Six months after the downtown parking garage opened, merchants say promised foot traffic never came
articles.dek: The $28 million structure on Palafox was sold as an economic engine for small businesses. Half a year in, some storefronts are darker than before.
brief: The 800-space Jefferson Street Garage opened in December 2025 after three years of construction and debate
Three storefronts within two blocks of the garage have closed since January; two more are listed for lease
City data shows the garage averages 34% occupancy on weekdays, well below the 60% projection used to justify the project
articles.body:
The sandwich board outside Mercer & Finch still promises "Free parking validation with purchase." The store behind it has been empty for six weeks.

Beth Anne Mercer locked the door to her women's clothing boutique on April 28, ending a seven-year run on South Palafox. She left the sign because she couldn't bring herself to take it down.

"I bought into it," Mercer said by phone from her parents' house in Mobile, where she's staying while figuring out what comes next. "The city told us the garage would bring thousands of people downtown every day. I hung on through three years of construction. Then I hung on six more months waiting for those people to show up."

They haven't. Not in the numbers anyone promised.

The numbers that mattered

When Pensacola City Council approved the Jefferson Street Garage in 2022, the pitch was straightforward. Downtown needed more parking. More parking meant more visitors. More visitors meant more spending.

The 800-space structure would cost $28 million, funded through a combination of Community Redevelopment Agency dollars and revenue bonds backed by projected parking fees. Consultants hired by the city estimated the garage would operate at 60% capacity within its first year, generating enough revenue to cover debt service while leaving room for eventual rate reductions.

A supplementary economic impact study projected the garage would add $4.2 million in annual retail spending within a three-block radius.

Six months in, the city's own data tells a different story.

Parking Services records obtained through a public records request show the Jefferson Street Garage averaged 34% occupancy on weekdays between January and May 2026. Weekend occupancy averaged 51%, buoyed by Saturday nights when downtown bars and restaurants draw crowds who don't arrive until after 9 p.m.

The $4.2 million spending projection assumed those capacity numbers would hold. It also assumed visitors would walk past storefronts on their way to wherever they were going.

The garage's primary pedestrian exit empties onto Jefferson Street, one block east of Palafox. Visitors heading to restaurants on the main strip can reach them without passing a single retail storefront.

Who's still here

On a Tuesday afternoon in early June, South Palafox between Garden and Main carries the quiet of a street that used to be busier.

At Coastal Books & Maps, owner David Restrepo sat behind the counter watching a ceiling fan turn. One customer had come in since lunch. She bought a $12 journal.

"I'm not going anywhere," Restrepo said. "I own the building. But if I was paying rent? I don't know."

He gestured toward the window. "You see that storefront across the street? That was a gift shop. Gone. Next to it was a jewelry place, local artist, beautiful stuff. Gone. And the shoe store on the corner, they're hanging on, but I know they're hurting."

Restrepo has been on Palafox for 14 years. He's seen cycles. The 2008 crash. The BP oil spill. The pandemic. Each time, he said, there was a clear cause and an eventual recovery.

"This is different. This is death by disappointment."

What the city says

City spokesperson Amanda Torres declined to make Parking Services Director Marcus Webb available for an interview. In a written statement, Torres said the garage "continues to serve a vital role in downtown's parking infrastructure" and that "utilization patterns are still stabilizing as residents and visitors become familiar with the facility."

The statement did not address the gap between projected and actual occupancy.

At the May 23 City Council meeting, Council member Jared Simmons asked City Administrator Keith Wilkins whether the garage was meeting expectations.

"We're tracking the numbers," Wilkins said. "It's early."

Simmons, who voted against the garage in 2022, pressed further. "At what point does 'early' become 'we missed'?"

Wilkins said staff would provide a comprehensive report at the one-year mark in December.

The validation problem

Part of the original pitch to downtown merchants was a validation program. Businesses could purchase validation stickers in bulk, then hand them to customers who would receive discounted parking rates.

The program launched in January. By March, Pensacola Downtown Improvement Board records show, only 11 businesses had enrolled. By May, three had dropped out.

"It's complicated," said Jennifer Wu, who owns a home goods store on Garden Street. "You buy these stickers, you give them out, the customer still has to walk to the garage, find the machine, figure out the interface. Half the time they just pay full price because it's easier."

Wu said she sold through her initial allocation of 200 stickers in two months, then didn't reorder. The program cost her about $600. She estimates it generated perhaps $200 in additional sales.

"The math doesn't work."

What comes next

The Downtown Improvement Board's quarterly merchant survey, released last week, showed 62% of responding businesses rated foot traffic as "below expectations" for the first half of 2026. That's up from 41% in the same period last year, when the garage was still under construction and merchants were anticipating its opening.

DIB Executive Director Thomas Keating said the board is "actively exploring strategies" to increase garage utilization and pedestrian flow. He mentioned potential wayfinding improvements, promotional partnerships with restaurants, and a possible summer concert series in the small plaza adjacent to the garage.

"We believe in downtown," Keating said. "We're not giving up."

But belief doesn't pay rent.

Carmen Santos has operated a Cuban restaurant on Intendencia Street for nine years. She's two blocks from the garage. Her lunch traffic is down 20% from this time last year.

"They told us to be patient during construction," Santos said, wiping down a table that hadn't been used since the breakfast rush. "They told us to be patient when it opened. Now they tell us to be patient while they figure out what went wrong."

She folded the rag and set it on the counter.

"I'm running out of patience. And I'm running out of time."

Down the street, the sandwich board outside Mercer & Finch caught the afternoon light. The validation offer still faced the sidewalk, waiting for customers who knew where else to park.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's newest training squadron is its smallest—and its future
articles.dek: The Navy's unmanned aerial systems program graduated its first class of drone operators last month. What that means for the base's next decade.
brief: Training Squadron 99 graduated its first 12 drone operators in May, marking the Navy's formal commitment to UAS training at NAS Pensacola
The program currently operates from a retrofitted hangar with 8 instructors and 6 training drones, but plans call for a $47 million expansion by 2030
Base commanders project UAS training could eventually account for 30% of all aviation training at Pensacola, reshaping the installation's role in naval aviation
articles.body:
The hangar sits at the far end of Radford Boulevard, past the T-6 Texans lined up on the flight line and the crush of student aviators in their green flight suits. No roar of turboprops here. Inside Hangar 1847, six small gray aircraft rest on wheeled cradles, each no bigger than a dining room table.

This is Training Squadron 99. Twelve sailors graduated from here last month. The Navy's future walked out the door carrying certificates instead of wings.

"We're not replacing pilots," said Cmdr. Jessica Thornton, the squadron's commanding officer. She stood in the hangar's main bay on a Tuesday morning, the concrete floor still cool. "We're building something that didn't exist five years ago."

A quiet arrival

VT-99 stood up in October 2025 with little ceremony. No band. No visiting admirals. Eight instructor pilots, a handful of enlisted maintainers and a training curriculum still being written.

The squadron operates the MQ-9B SeaGuardian and a smaller trainer variant designed specifically for the schoolhouse. Students spend 14 weeks learning sensor operation, flight planning and the peculiar art of flying something you can't feel—no stick forces, no seat-of-the-pants feedback, just screens and data.

"It's flying, but it's not," said Lt. j.g. Marcus Webb, 24, one of the May graduates. He sat in the squadron's ready room, a space that looks more like an IT office than a traditional aviator's den. Fewer leather chairs. More monitors. "You have to trust the system in a way that takes getting used to."

Webb will head to a fleet squadron in Jacksonville next month. He applied for UAS training after washing out of the jet pipeline—not for lack of ability, he said, but because the unmanned track seemed like where the Navy was actually headed.

The numbers tell a story

NAS Pensacola trained approximately 1,800 student naval aviators last year through its primary and intermediate training pipelines. VT-99 graduated 12.

That ratio will shift.

According to planning documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request, Chief of Naval Air Training projects the UAS pipeline will grow to 200 annual graduates by 2030. The documents outline a $47 million military construction project to build a dedicated UAS training facility on the base's north side, replacing the current retrofitted hangar.

Capt. William Reeves, NAS Pensacola's commanding officer, confirmed the expansion plans in an interview last week.

"The secretary's guidance is clear," Reeves said. "Unmanned systems are a priority. Pensacola is where naval aviators have trained for over a century. This is the natural home for this mission."

The new facility would include simulator bays, a dedicated ground control station training area and expanded hangar space for up to 24 aircraft. Construction is slated to begin in fiscal year 2028, pending congressional appropriation.

What changes, what doesn't

Walk through the National Naval Aviation Museum on any given Saturday and you'll see the artifacts of a manned aviation culture built over generations. The Hellcats and Corsairs. The Blue Angels' A-4 Skyhawks. Photos of young men in leather helmets learning to land on pitching carrier decks.

Unmanned aviation doesn't generate the same mythology. There are no drone aces. No call signs painted on fuselages.

Thornton acknowledged the cultural tension.

"There's pride in what came before. There should be," she said. "But the threats are changing. The platforms have to change too."

The Navy has been slower than the Air Force to embrace unmanned systems for combat aviation. The MQ-25 Stingray tanker drone entered fleet service in 2024, but it refuels manned aircraft—it doesn't replace them. The SeaGuardian fills surveillance and maritime patrol roles, work previously done by manned P-3 Orions and P-8 Poseidons.

Whether unmanned aircraft will eventually perform strike missions from carrier decks remains a matter of debate in Pentagon circles. What's clear is that someone has to operate them. And increasingly, that training will happen in Pensacola.

The local calculus

For the base and the community around it, the UAS expansion represents both continuity and change.

NAS Pensacola employs approximately 16,000 military and civilian personnel and generates an estimated $5.1 billion in annual economic impact for the region, according to the most recent figures from the Pensacola Chamber of Commerce. The base has survived multiple rounds of Base Realignment and Closure reviews by emphasizing its training mission.

New missions mean new justification.

"Every time there's a BRAC conversation, communities get nervous," said Dr. Sarah Chen, an economist at the University of West Florida who studies military community relations. "A growing training pipeline is the best insurance policy a base can have."

The construction project would bring temporary jobs. The expanded squadron would bring permanent ones—more instructors, more maintainers, more support staff.

Not everyone is enthusiastic. Some residents near the base's north boundary have raised concerns about increased drone flights, though the training aircraft are far quieter than the T-6 turboprops that have buzzed Pensacola's skies for decades.

"We're working with the community," Reeves said. "The footprint is modest compared to our existing operations."

Watching and waiting

On a clear morning last week, a SeaGuardian lifted off from Runway 26 and turned south toward the Gulf. From the ground, it looked like a large model airplane, climbing in silence.

Inside the ground control station—a converted shipping container with air conditioning and too many screens—two student operators tracked its progress. One flew. One monitored sensors. An instructor watched over their shoulders.

The drone would orbit for four hours, practicing the kind of long-duration surveillance work that wears out human pilots. It landed without incident.

"Good sortie," the instructor said.

No drama. No roaring engines. No victory roll.

Just another day in a training squadron that barely existed a year ago and might define naval aviation's next chapter.

Webb, the recent graduate, said he thinks about that sometimes.

"People ask if it feels like real flying," he said. "I tell them it's real because it matters. The mission is real. The threat is real." He paused. "The rest is just how you get there."
